newsitem.title: USA: Americas' gold output up 6.1 pct in 1996 - GFMS.
newsitem.headline: Americas' gold output up 6.1 pct in 1996 - GFMS.

text.p: Output from both North American and Latin American gold mines rose by 6.1 percent in 1996, compared with a rise in world mine supply of 3.3 percent, according to Gold Fields Mineral Services Ltd's 1997 survey of the world gold industry published Wednesday.

"The rise (in mine output) was fuelled in part by growth in three of the traditional 'Big Four' producing countries, namely Australia, Canada and the U.S., while emerging producers in Latin America and South East Asia generated eight and nine percent growth respectively," one of the reports author's Philip Klapwijk said.
Total U.S. gold production rose to 329.3 tonnes in 1996 from 319.0 tonnes in 1995, while Canadian output rose to 163.9 tonnes from 150.3 tonnes the previous year.

Total Latin American gold output was 304.5 tonnes, up from 282.10 tonnes in 1995, with Peru taking over the lead as the largest regional producer from Brazil. Peru output rose to 64.8 tonnes from 57.4 tonnes the precious year.
Highlight of the 1996 year in the U.S. was the start of underground operations at the Meikle mine, with output expected to exceed 12 tonnes a year.

Opposition from environmental lobbyists to proposed new mining projects in the U.S. contined unabated, resulting in at least one case in the cancellation of a project at the New World copper-gold-silver deposit near Yellowstone, the report said.

"One result of the stringent criteria applied to the preparation of environmental impact studies is the increasing amount of time required to obtain the necessary permits for mining," the report said.
The average total permitting time required is currently estimated to be around five years.

While the search for new gold reserves has encouraged further globalization, many American companies have directed substantial portions of their exploration budgets to increasing reserves at existing operations in the U.S., particularly in Nevada and Alaska.

"As part of this process, a number of companies are evaluating the feasibility of developing underground desposits underlying existing open pits, as the economies associated with a transition to underground mining often make this route preferable to developing new surface deposits," the report said.
At present though less than 20 percent of gold output in the U.S. is generated at underground operations.
Canadian production rose for the second consecutive year, reaching 164 tonnes, as a result of significant increases in output at existing mines such as Golden Giant and Eskay Creek.
Three medium sized mines also began operations - Troilus, Holloway and Komis, but will really only add to Canadian output in 1997.
Latin American production has risen 50 percent in the past decade to just over 300 tonnes and growth is likely to continue into the next century, the report said.
"The growth in the Peruvian mining industry has been quite phenomenal, with gold output increasing 500 percent in the last 10 years," the report said.
Much of this rise is attributable to the contribution from Newmont and Buenaventura's low-cost Yanacocha mine, where output exceeded 25 tonnes last year.
Chile's gold production registered its third consecutive annual increase, rising 16 percent to 56 tonnes.
Most of this increase came from Amax and Bema Gold's Refugio mine in Maricunga begun in 1996, while Andacollo, Pimenton and Fachinal increased output also after start-ups in 1995.
By contrast Brazil's production continued to decline, though output from the formal mining sector, dominated by the state-owned Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), stabilized around 41 tonnes.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641))
